newsitem.title: USA: San Francisco sues BankAmerica over bonds.
newsitem.headline: San Francisco sues BankAmerica over bonds.

text.p: San Francisco said Thursday it sued BankAmerica Corp's Bank of America for more than $12 million, alleging it mishandled municipal bond funds.

City Attorney Louise Renne said the complaint, filed in Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges that the bank, acting as a trustee, mishandled bond funds issued for low-income housing, schools, fire protection and other public works.
The bonds were issued by the city, the San Francisco School District, the San Francisco Housing Authority and the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency.
"The bank has breached the public's trust," Renne said in a statement. "The evidence we have of mismanagement and cover-up will shock the harshest critic of the banking industry."

The city said its legal action takes the form of a complaint to intervene in a "whistleblower" action filed under seal in April 1995. The "whistleblower" who filed the complaint is Patrick Stull, a former vice-president for corporate trust at Bank of America.
The city attorney's office said it has been investigating Stull's allegations in cooperation with Stull and the California Attorney-General's office.
Stull's lawsuit is no longer under seal.
The state Attorney General's office said earlier that the state of California has been conducting its own investigation of Bank of America.

"The state has been involved in an investigation with Bank of America for several months," said Rob Stutzman, a spokesman for the state Attorney General. "The state is in the process of mediating the findings of that investigation."
The state's Attorney General office declined to discuss the nature of the state investigation.
But state sources involved in the probe said California's investigation of Bank of America involves alleged overbilling for trustee services.

Renne said the city's reconstruction of its losses was not yet complete. She said the current figure of $12 million in actual losses could easily reach $17 million or more, adding that the city could be entitled to three times the actual proven damages if the city prevails in the lawsuit.

San Francisco's suit alleges that Bank of America lost control on a "massive scale" of hundreds of millions of dollars in bond funds entrusted to the bank so that the bank did not know how much cash it should have on hand or how much money was owed to bond holders.

The suit also alleges Bank of America began in 1989 to "force-balance" the bond accounts by arbitrarily eliminating the records of outstanding bonds, coupons and checks and by creating false records to show that the outstanding bonds and coupons had been paid when in fact they had not.

In addition, Renne said the lawsuit alleges the bank charged fees for services the bank did not perform and double charged for services it did perform, and engaged in a "massive cover-up, lost and destroyed records, (and) sent false monthly reports to its customers."
The suit also alleged Bank of America kept for itself millions of dollars of unclaimed payments of interest on bonds and made unauthorized investments with funds the bank was holding in trust.
A Bank of America spokesman said he has yet to see San Francisco's lawsuit.
"We've seen rumors of a lawsuit but we have not seen an actual lawsuit," Bank of America spokesman Peter Magnani said.
He said Bank of America has been in negotiations with the city of San Francisco and the state of California "over activities related to a business we no longer own."
Magnani added: "We do not think our exposure in this matter is material."
